conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these first weeks with your baby. We’re going to use a short, well-trusted tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and we’ll take it one gentle question at a time. Ready to begin?

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the things you used to look forward to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I’ve noticed I don’t get as excited about things as I used to—like, my sister offered to watch the baby so I could meet a friend for coffee, and I went, but it felt kind of… flat. I still enjoy little moments with the baby, but most stuff feels like I’m just going through the motions rather than really looking forward to anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when the baby makes those silly milk-drunk faces. It’s not the same big belly laugh I used to have, but if something’s genuinely funny, I’ll chuckle. It just feels a little muted, like the volume’s turned down.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I *should* feel excited about little plans—like taking the baby for his check-up or having my mom over—but mostly it just feels like another task on the list. I don’t get that happy “can’t-wait” feeling I used to have before he was born.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… like yesterday he was fussy for almost an hour and I kept thinking it must be because I missed some cue or my milk isn’t “good enough.” Logically I know babies just cry, but my head still jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” It’s not all day, but it happens more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him spitting up and choking, or I’ll worry that a tiny cough means he’s getting sick. Nothing’s actually wrong, but my heart races until I check his breathing or take his temperature. It usually passes pretty quick—I can talk myself down—but yeah, it pops up most days.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panic… more like a sudden “what-if” rush. Like the other night I was rocking him and out of nowhere I imagined dropping him on the hardwood. My stomach flipped, I got that cold sweat feeling, and I had to sit down and hug him tight. It lasted maybe a minute, then it was gone, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when the laundry pile looks bigger than the baby and I can’t even get a shower in—my brain feels foggy and I think, “How am I supposed to keep us both alive if I can’t even find a clean onesie?” I usually manage once I make a quick list and tackle one thing at a time, but it feels overwhelming in the moment.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Sleep itself isn’t too bad—once I’m out, I stay out till he wakes to feed. It’s the getting-to-sleep part that’s rough. When the house is quiet my mind replays everything I think I messed up that day, and I’ll lie there 20-30 minutes feeling tense. I’m not up crying or anything, just can’t switch off right away.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel kind of down some stretches of the day—like this heavy blanket settles over me and everything feels gray. It’s not all day, and I haven’t had any hopeless thoughts, but I’ve caught myself tearing up while folding onesies a couple of times this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried… maybe twice in the past week. Once was when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like my body was failing him, and the other time was after a phone call when my partner jokingly asked if I’d “done anything productive today.” It wasn’t sobbing, just tears that came and went after a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that the joy you once expected hasn't fully arrived since your baby came. While you can still smile at his milk-drunk faces, most plans feel flat and routine; you blame yourself quickly when he fusses, worry about unlikely dangers, and sometimes feel a sudden rush of fear or the sense that daily tasks are piling too high. Nights bring a restless mind and moments of quiet tears, yet you have not felt any wish to harm yourself and you continue to care devotedly for your little one.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—recognises she "should" feel excited but no longer experiences the "can't-wait" feeling, matching "Definitely less than I used to".</sym>, <sym>"Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive worries occurring "most days," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Sudden intrusive thought about dropping baby, physical panic symptoms (cold sweat, shaky) but brief duration maps to 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent episodes of feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks, though she eventually manages with coping strategies, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes noticeable sadness that comes and goes but is present multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 15 (≥14 indicates probable major depression under peripartum specifier). The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (Q2 score 2), <sym>feelings of worthlessness/inappropriate guilt</sym> (Q3 score 2), <sym>anxiety</sym> (Q4 score 2) and <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> (Q5 score 2), <sym>reduced ability to cope</sym> (Q6 score 2), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> (Q7 score 1), and <sym>depressed mood</sym> (Q8 score 2; Q9 score 1). Duration >2 weeks, clinically significant distress, and functional impact meet screening threshold for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation (Q10 score 0) lowers immediate safety risk but does not negate need for evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next week for full assessment and treatment planning
2. Continue usual supports-family help, rest when baby sleeps, balanced meals-and note any worsening mood, new panic attacks, or thoughts of self-harm, then seek care immediately
3. Consider joining a new-mother support group (local or virtual) to share experiences and reduce isolation
4. Use brief self-care tools: 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when sudden worry or panic sensations arise; limit evening screen time to improve sleep onset
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2-4 weeks (or sooner if symptoms escalate) to monitor progress after treatment initiation
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Screening Note – 2 wk postpartum  
Date: ___

Presenting symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate intensity):  
- Anhedonia / reduced enjoyment (Q2)  
- Intermittent low mood, “heavy” or “gray” periods, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Initial insomnia secondary to rumination (Q7)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting adequacy (Q3)  
- Intrusive “what-if” fears, brief nocturnal panic sensations without full panic attacks (Q4, Q5)  
- Periodic sense of being overwhelmed; difficulty coping with daily tasks (Q6)  

Pattern: Symptoms clustered in late afternoon/evening, resolve partially with distraction or support; no functional impairment in basic self/baby care.  

Safety: Denies self-harm or thoughts of harm to infant (Q10).  

Screening significance: Meets partial criteria for Perinatal Depression and Anxiety; severity below threshold for major depressive episode but exceeds “baby-blues” duration.  
Risk factors: Primiparity, sleep fragmentation, high self-expectations of motherhood.  

Plan: Routine Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to quantify; review in 1 week or sooner if worsening mood, panic, or suicidal ideation emerges.
